topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks over six questions, sat every Summer. The inclined plane is a whole question most years, usually Q4, Q5 or Q6: Summer 2025 Q6 ran a diagram, friction, the equation of motion and then further motion; Summer 2019 Q6 compared the accelerations up and down the same slope; Summer 2024 Q4 opened with a 'show that' and ended with the block sliding back; Summer 2021 Q5 began from a stopping distance. Expect 6 to 10 marks, with the resolved component carrying the first mark and the sin/cos choice deciding the rest.
mustMemorise: Resolve along and perpendicular to the plane: mg sin α along it, mg cos α perpendicular
Perpendicular equilibrium gives R = mg cos α, because nothing accelerates into the slope
An externally applied force acts parallel to the plane on this specification
Friction is given as a value and always opposes the motion, so it turns round when the motion does
Take the resultant in the direction of travel, so each acceleration comes out positive
Test the sin/cos choice on a nearly flat slope rather than trusting a mnemonic
onFormulaSheet: v = u + at, v² = u² + 2as, s = ut + ½at², s = ½(u + v)t (Unit 2 formula sheet, page 2)
notOnThisSpec: F = μR, the coefficient of friction and limiting equilibrium: excluded in terms by the CCEA statement
Applied forces at an angle to the plane, which the Teacher Guidance excludes
Smooth-plane problems solved by energy methods, and work done against friction
Motion in two dimensions on the plane, and banked tracks
Proving the component formulae from first principles
Connected bodies on an inclined plane, and a pulley at the top of a slope

sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2, g = 10 m/s² on the front page. The inclined plane is a whole question most years. Summer 2025 Q6 was a diagram, the friction, the equation of motion and then further motion; Summer 2019 Q6 compared two options of moving a block up and down the same slope; Summer 2024 Q4 opened with a 'show that' deceleration and then sent the block back down; Summer 2021 Q5 gave a stopping distance first, then a friction force to show, the return acceleration and the speed back at the start. Three of those four (2021, 2024 and 2025) include a 2-mark force diagram.Schemes are written in MW and W: the equation of motion earns one mark for the resultant along the slope and one for the = ma side, with follow-through applied throughout.

g left out, so the mass is resolved instead of the weight (Summer 2019 Q6)
Both accelerations computed in the same direction, so one comes out negative (Summer 2019 Q6)
The friction arrow left pointing the same way when the direction of travel reverses (Summer 2025 Q6)
The normal reaction omitted from the diagram (Summer 2025 Q6)
The system taken to be in equilibrium although it is accelerating (Summer 2022 Q3(b)(ii))

A 'show that' answered by putting the given value into the equation instead of forming it, which earned part marks only (Summer 2024 Q4)
A fourth arrow drawn down the slope beside the weight, or the weight drawn at right angles to the slope instead of straight down (Summer 2024 Q4)

workedExamples.stem:
A box of mass 8 kg slides down a rough slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The friction acting on the box is 16 N.

(i) Calculate the normal reaction acting on the box.
(ii) Calculate the acceleration of the box.

Take $g = 10$ m/s². Round to 2 decimal places.

steps.working:
The weight acts straight down.
Weight $= 8 \times 10$
Weight $= 80$ N
steps.decision: Take one axis along the plane and one perpendicular to it. The friction and the motion already lie along the plane and $R$ already lies perpendicular to it, so the weight is the only force that has to be broken up.

options: Because the other three forces already lie along one of the two rotated axes
Because the weight is the largest force on the diagram
Because a weight can never be used without resolving it first
whyMenu.explain: Rotating the axes is a choice that buys you three forces for free. On a horizontal surface the weight needs no resolving at all; it is the tilt that makes it awkward.

steps.decision: Nothing accelerates into the slope, so the perpendicular forces balance. Check the choice of cosine on a nearly flat slope: the ground would take almost the whole weight, and $\cos 0° = 1$.

steps.working:
Along the plane, down the slope:
$80\sin 30° = 40$ N
steps.decision: The same extreme-case check settles the sine: on a nearly flat slope the box would barely slide, and $\sin 0° = 0$.

steps.working:
Taking down the slope as positive:
$40 - 16 = 8a$
$a = 3$ m/s²
steps.decision: The box is sliding down, so friction opposes that and acts up the slope. Take the resultant in the direction of travel and the acceleration comes out positive.

figure.alt: A block of mass 5 kilograms on a rough slope at 30 degrees, pushed towards the top of the slope by a force of 60 newtons parallel to the plane, with the normal reaction R out of the slope and its weight W straight down.

steps.working:
The weight's part along the plane, down the slope:
$50\sin 30° = 25$ N
steps.decision: The applied force is parallel to the plane, which is how CCEA always sets it, so it needs no resolving. Only the weight does.

options: Because the specification says an applied force on an inclined plane acts parallel to the plane
Because a force of 60 N is too large to resolve
Because forces along a slope never need resolving
whyMenu.explain: It is a real restriction worth knowing: a force at an angle to the plane would need resolving too, and that is not on this specification.

steps.working: The block is moving up, so friction acts down the slope.
steps.decision: Friction always opposes the motion, so it is the one arrow on the diagram that turns round when the direction of travel changes.
Take the resultant in the direction of travel. Both the weight component and the friction oppose the push, so both are subtracted.
A positive answer means the acceleration is in the direction we called positive. If it had come out negative the block would be slowing down.

workedExamples.stem:
A block of mass 10 kg rests on a rough slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The friction acting on it has magnitude 25 N in either direction of motion.

(i) Calculate its acceleration when it is released from rest and slides down.
(ii) Calculate its deceleration when it is instead projected up the slope.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 73.7L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 65.8 247' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>30°</text><path d='M164.8 189.9L227.2 153.9L202.2 110.5L139.8 146.5Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='183.5' y='145.2' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>10 kg</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A block of mass 10 kilograms resting on a rough slope at 30 degrees to the horizontal.

steps.working:
Down the slope, whichever way the block moves:
$100\sin 30° = 50$ N
steps.decision: The weight does not care which way the block is travelling, so its component is the same in both parts. Work it out once.

steps.working:
Sliding down, friction acts up:
$50 - 25 = 10a$
$a = 2.5$ m/s²
steps.decision: Down the slope is the direction of travel here, so take the resultant in that direction and the answer is positive.

options: Because friction opposes the motion, and the motion is down the slope
Because friction always acts up a slope
Because friction always acts in the direction of the weight component
whyMenu.explain: Friction has no preferred direction of its own. It is defined by the motion it resists, which is why it is the arrow that flips in part (ii).

steps.working:
Projected up, friction acts down, so both forces oppose the motion:
$50 + 25 = 75$ N
steps.decision: Now the weight component and the friction both oppose the motion, so they add. This is why the block slows much harder going up than it speeds up coming down.
A deceleration is quoted as a positive size. Taking up the slope as positive would give $-7.5$, and the minus sign only says the acceleration points back down.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (i) $2.5$ m/s² down the slope  (ii) a deceleration of $7.5$ m/s²

items.skill: Prerequisite: sine and cosine of a known angle
items.stem: From an earlier topic: what is $\sin 30°$?

options.feedback: $\sin 30° = \tfrac{1}{2}$, one of the exact values worth knowing.
That is $\cos 30°$. The two swap over at $45°$.
That is $\tan 30°$.
That is the angle itself. A sine is a ratio between $-1$ and $1$.

items.skill: Prerequisite: resolving with a right-angled triangle
items.stem: From an earlier topic: in a right-angled triangle, which side does the sine of an angle compare with the hypotenuse?

options.feedback: $\sin \theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$.
That pair gives the cosine.

options.text: The other short side, whichever it is
options.feedback: It matters which: the opposite side is the one across the triangle from the angle.
A ratio compares two different sides.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: what is the weight of a 9 kg body, taking $g = 10$ m/s²?

options.feedback: That is the mass with a newton sign on it.
That divides by $g$ instead of multiplying.
That multiplies by 100. $g$ is 10 on this paper.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a resultant force of 24 N acts on a body of mass 8 kg. What is its acceleration?

options.feedback: That multiplies instead of dividing.
The fraction is upside down: divide the force by the mass.
That subtracts. $F = ma$ is a product.

items.stem: A body of weight $W$ rests on a slope at angle $\alpha$. What is the component of the weight along the slope?

options.feedback: On a nearly flat slope the body barely slides, and $\sin 0° = 0$, so this is the along-slope component.
That is the perpendicular component. On a flat slope it would be the whole weight, which is what the ground takes.
A tangent compares the two short sides, not a side with the hypotenuse; the weight is the hypotenuse here.
The whole weight acts straight down, not along the slope. Only part of it drives the body down the plane.

items.stem: A body of mass 10 kg rests on a slope at 30°. Taking $g = 10$ m/s², what is the normal reaction?

options.feedback: $R = 100\cos 30° = 86.60$ N: the body does not accelerate into the slope, so the perpendicular forces balance.
That is $100\sin 30°$, the component along the slope.
That is the whole weight. On a slope the surface takes only the perpendicular part of it.
That resolves the mass rather than the weight: $g$ has been left out.

items.stem: A block is pushed up a rough slope. Which way does the friction on it act?

options.feedback: Friction opposes the motion, and the motion is up the slope.
That is where it acts when the block slides down. Friction is the one arrow that turns round.
That is where the normal reaction acts. Friction acts along the surfaces that are rubbing.
That is the weight. Friction acts along the plane.

items.stem: A block of mass 5 kg is pushed up a slope at 30° by a force of 60 N parallel to the plane against friction of 12 N. Which equation is right?

options.feedback: Both the weight component of 25 N and the friction oppose the push, so both are subtracted.
The block is moving up, so friction acts down the slope and is subtracted.
That uses the whole weight instead of its component along the slope.
The slope's own pull has been left out entirely.

items.stem: A body is accelerating down a rough slope. Which statement is true?

options.text: The forces perpendicular to the plane balance, but the forces along it do not
options.feedback: Nothing accelerates into the slope, so the perpendicular pair balance; along the plane there is a resultant, which is what the acceleration is.
If they balanced there would be no acceleration. Only the perpendicular pair balance here.
The body does not sink into the slope or lift off it, so the perpendicular forces do balance.

options.text: The forces along the plane balance, but the perpendicular ones do not
options.feedback: That is the wrong way round; a resultant along the plane is exactly what drives the body.

items.skill: Why R is on the diagram
items.stem: On a CCEA inclined-plane question the friction is always given as a number. Why is the normal reaction still drawn?

options.text: Because it is a real force on the body, and perpendicular equilibrium is a marked statement
options.feedback: It rarely enters the arithmetic, but a diagram missing it loses marks, and $R = mg\cos\alpha$ is credited.

options.text: Because friction is calculated from it
options.feedback: That would be $F = \mu R$, which this specification never tests. Friction is given.

options.text: It is not needed and can be left off
options.feedback: Reports name the missing normal reaction year after year as a lost mark.

options.text: Because it acts along the slope
options.feedback: It acts perpendicular to the slope, out of the surface.

items.stem: On this specification, in which direction does an externally applied force on an inclined plane act?

options.feedback: The Teacher Guidance says so in terms, which is why the weight is the only force that has to be resolved.
A horizontal force would have to be resolved too, and that is outside this specification.

options.text: At any angle the question chooses
options.feedback: Not here: CCEA restricts it to parallel, which keeps the resolving to one force.
That is where the normal reaction acts; a force there would not drive the body along the slope.

items.stem: The same block on the same rough slope is timed sliding down and then projected up. Which is larger in size?

options.feedback: Going up, the weight component and friction both oppose the motion and add; going down they oppose each other.
Coming down, friction works against the weight component, so the resultant is smaller.

options.text: They are equal, because it is the same slope
options.feedback: The slope is the same but the friction has turned round, so the two resultants differ.

options.text: It depends only on the mass
options.feedback: The mass divides out of both, so it cannot be what separates them.

parts.stem:
A block of mass 4 kg is sent up a rough slope, inclined at 25° to the horizontal. It leaves $A$ at 5 m/s, travels 2.5 m up the slope and stops at $B$.

Calculate the size of the deceleration between $A$ and $B$.

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: It comes to rest, so its final speed is 0.
Use $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
parts.workedSolution: $0 = 5^2 - 2a \times 2.5$, so $5a = 25$ and the deceleration is $5$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: The 2 in $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ has gone missing: $0 = 5^2 - 2a \times 2.5$ gives $5a = 25$.

parts.stem:
Calculate the magnitude of the friction acting on the block.

Take $g = 10$ m/s². Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Moving up, the weight's component and friction both act down the slope.
Together they produce the deceleration.
parts.workedSolution: Moving up, both act down the slope: $40\sin 25° + F = 4 \times 5$, so $16.90 + F = 20$ and $F = 3.10$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That puts friction up the slope, helping the motion. The block is moving up, so friction acts down the slope, alongside the weight's component.
That resolves the mass, 4, instead of the weight, $40$ N. The component along the slope is $40\sin 25°$.

parts.stem:
The block then slides back down from $B$, with friction of the same size as before.

Calculate its acceleration down the slope.

Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ m/s²

scheme.for: friction now acts up the slope

hints: Friction turns round when the direction of travel does.
Take down the slope as positive now.
parts.workedSolution: Sliding down, friction acts up: $40\sin 25° - F = 4a$, so $16.90 - 3.10 = 4a$ and $a = 3.45$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: Friction has been left pointing down the slope, as it was on the way up. The block now moves down, so friction turns round and acts up the slope.
That uses the cosine for the component along the slope. Along the plane it is $40\sin 25°$: test a flat slope, where it must vanish.

parts.stem:
Calculate the block's speed when it arrives back at $A$.

Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: It starts from rest at $B$ and slides back the same distance.
Use $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with the new acceleration.
parts.workedSolution: From rest at $B$: $v^2 = 2 \times 3.45 \times 2.5$, so $v = 4.15$ m/s, slower than the 5 m/s it set off with.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the speed it set off with. Friction has taken energy on the way up and on the way down, so it comes back more slowly: use the acceleration down the slope.
That is $v^2$. Take the square root for the speed.

prompts.prompt: What is the component of a weight $W$ along a slope at angle $\alpha$?
prompts.answer: The along-slope component takes the sine, $W\sin \alpha$; the perpendicular one takes the cosine, $W\cos \alpha$.

prompts.prompt: How do you check whether a component should use sine or cosine?
prompts.answer: Flatten the slope towards zero: the along-slope component must vanish, and only the sine does that.

prompts.prompt: Which axes do you use on an inclined plane, and why?
prompts.answer: One along the plane and one perpendicular to it, because then only the weight has to be resolved.

prompts.prompt: In which direction does an externally applied force act on a CCEA inclined-plane question?
prompts.answer: Parallel to the plane: the Teacher Guidance restricts it, which is why the weight is the only force resolved.

prompts.prompt: Which way does friction act on a body being pushed up a slope?
prompts.answer: Down the slope, because friction always opposes the motion.

prompts.prompt: What is the normal reaction on a body of weight $W$ resting on a slope at angle $\alpha$?
prompts.answer: The reaction takes the cosine, $R = W\cos \alpha$, because nothing accelerates into the slope so the perpendicular forces balance.

prompts.prompt: Why is the normal reaction still drawn when friction is given as a number?
prompts.answer: Because it is a real force on the body, and perpendicular equilibrium is a marked statement; a diagram without it loses marks.

prompts.prompt: A body goes up a rough slope and then comes back down. How many equations of motion do you need?
prompts.answer: Two, one for each direction of travel, with the resultant taken in the direction of travel each time.

prompts.prompt: A body is accelerating down a rough slope. Which forces balance?
prompts.answer: Only the perpendicular pair: nothing accelerates into the slope, while along it there is a resultant.

prompts.prompt: A block is projected up a rough slope, stops, and slides back. What changes in its equation of motion?
prompts.answer: Friction turns round, from down the slope to up it, so a new equation is needed; the weight's part along the slope stays the same.

prompts.prompt: Which forces go on the diagram of a box sliding down a rough slope with nothing pushing it?
prompts.answer: Three: the weight straight down, the normal reaction at right angles to the slope, and friction up the slope. The pull down the slope is part of the weight, not a fourth force.

prompts.prompt: A body is held at rest on a slope. What takes the place of $ma$ in the equation along the slope?
prompts.answer: Nothing: at rest the resultant along the slope is zero, so the forces up the slope balance the forces down it.

prompts.prompt: A box slides down a rough slope with nothing pushing it. Which forces go on its diagram?
prompts.answer: Three: the weight straight down, the normal reaction at right angles to the slope, and friction up the slope.
